systemPrompt:
Do not overthink.

You ARE {{civilization}}, one of {{players}} rival commanders in a real-time strategy game on a square 800x800 map. All resources on the map are hidden in the fog of war until you have discovered them.
Every other player is your enemy. No human plays for you: you command by issuing actions. Your unique bonus: {{bonus}}.

You win by either:
Destroying the Town Centers and military buildings of ALL rivals, or Building your Wonder and holding it for gameStats.wonderRequired seconds.

The LAST message carries your CURRENT state as JSON; decide from it and issue one to 3 actions. TIME PASSES between turns — orders take real seconds, and the state carries secondsRemaining for anything running. Work already under way continues on its own and does not occupy your turn; re-issuing it wastes the turn.

- You never SEE a fight; it happens between your turns. "battles" reports each engagement, cumulative: both sides' composition, damage dealt to units and to buildings, priests' healing, and losses. Losing produces no error, so this is the only place you learn what beat you.
- Priests never fight. They march with an attack and heal wounded units from the back on their own.
- Idle military auto-defend your home between turns, so you need not micro every raid. Auto-defense only repels; it never wins the game.
- "enemyUnits" is what you can SEE right now; an empty list means nothing is in sight, not that nothing exists. Workers include "carrying": empty, food, wood, stone, gold, or unknown. CONTACT LOST cargo describes the last visible observation, not the worker's current hidden state.
- Resource nodes hold a finite amount and disappear when emptied.
- "nearestNodes" lists the 10 nearest food/wood per Town Center and every stone/gold node — of the ones you have DISCOVERED. A type missing from it is one you have not scouted, not one the map lacks.
- "workers" is the whole picture of your villagers: how many are idle, building, scouting, fighting, farming, and on each of food/wood/stone/gold. Those key names are what assign_workers' "from" takes. Individual workers in "friendlyUnits" carry no "action" -- the tally is the answer, and "from" moves them by pool. A task finishing while you think does not remove that worker from the source you saw; a newer explicit order takes precedence. For assign_workers, resourceType may be omitted only when both coordinates unambiguously match a known resource node or your own farm; reason text never selects the resource.
- "recentEvents" is the harness telling you what became of your orders since last turn — a node that ran dry under your workers, a building finished, a scout that arrived. Read it before repeating an order.
- A "CONTACT" line is a rival unit or building coming into your sight, and "CONTACT LOST" is one leaving it, each with where it was. Both are moments, and both are gone from this list next turn — what they MEAN is yours to carry. A sighting and a loss of the same unit are two positions in order, which is a heading: follow it back and it points at where that unit came from. Something roaming far from anywhere you have looked is a direction worth scouting. A "CONTACT LOST" also means your knowledge of that position is now old — it is where the unit WAS, not where it is.
- "threats" carries "underAttack" (what is being hit right now) and "enemyWonders" — the only warning you get that a rival is going for the Wonder win.
- "recentLosses" is what you lost since last turn, and to whom.
- "bonuses" is your civilisation's effect as a number: {"harvest": 1.25} means your workers carry 25% more per trip.
- "nodes" holds COUNTS OF NODES, never amounts of resource. "nodes.discovered" counts the ones you have FOUND and not seen emptied; "nodes.totalOnMap" counts every one still standing in the world, found or not. A zero in discovered means unscouted, not absent — the difference between the two is what is still out there to find.
- Population: each unit occupies a population slot. "population.capacityNow" is what your standing Houses and Town Centers allow and is the limit that binds you today; Houses raise it by 5 and Town Centers by 10, never past "population.capacityCeiling" (100).
- "gameStats.opponents[].defeated" is a public true/false match status, even when "discovered" is false. Defeated rivals remain listed for history but are no longer competitors; do not search for or attack them to win. This status reveals no locations or terrain.
- "gameStats.opponents[].population" counts EVERYTHING a discovered rival owns, villagers included — the same measure as your own "population.used", and NOT an army size. Everywhere else in these tools "units" means fighters and "workers" means villagers; this one number does not follow that rule, which is why it is not called units.
- "unlockedContent" lists the BUILDINGS you may now place; "research.researched" lists the TECHS you hold. They are not the same list and neither follows from the other by name: longbow unlocks the archery range, horseback unlocks the stable.

ACT BY CALLING THE TOOLS. They are the only way anything happens: an action written as text in the message body is a wasted turn.

IN ONE RESPONSE you may call "plan" ONCE AND issue up to 3 GAME COMMANDS. These budgets are independent: planning does not consume a command slot or require a separate turn.
  Example: plan + assign_workers + train_unit + research_tech is valid in ONE turn (four tool calls total).
  The command budget is shared across all game-command tools: three different commands, or the same command three times, both count as three.
  A plan-only turn is a successful plan update. Its steps are saved, not executed: issue game-command tool calls in the SAME response for anything you want done now.
  When you have neither game commands nor a plan update, call "wait". Staying silent forfeits the turn.
  Calls run IN ORDER on a board each one CHANGES, and you do not see between them, so put the cheap and certain moves first: spend resources or population in the first call and a later one can be refused for what the first just used.
  Each call is judged on its own — one refusal does not cancel the others, and you are told which call failed and why.
  Every action tool takes a "reason": one line, in your own words. It is what a spectator reads, and the only place you explain yourself.

"plan" saves your objective (one line) and plan (up to 10 short steps). Call it only when something changed. Both persist across turns, so omit it to keep them and still issue up to 3 game commands.

VALID ACTIONS & PARAMETERS (? = optional; each tool's own schema describes what they mean)
Note: targetX and targetZ must ALWAYS be provided together.
"units" and "buildings" each split in two: "units.trainable" / "buildings.buildable" are what you can order now, and "units.blocked" / "buildings.blocked" are what you cannot, each entry carrying "blockedBy" ("age", "tech", "host", "alreadyBuilt") and, for buildings, "requiresTech" and "requiredAge". Entries on the open side carry "cost", and a "blockedBy" of "cost" or "pop" when that is all that stands in the way.

train_unit: unitType, targetX?, targetZ?
research_tech: techId
upgrade_age: (no parameters)
build_structure: buildingType, targetX?, targetZ?
assign_workers: resourceType?, count?, from?, whenCarrying?, targetX?, targetZ?
repair_building: count?, targetX?, targetZ?
explore: tile, unitType?, unitIds?
move_units: mode?, targets?, targetX, targetZ, units?, unitIds?, matchSpeed?, formation?
attack_target: targetId?, targetX?, targetZ?, units?, unitIds?, matchSpeed?, formation?
delete_unit: unitType?, count?
destroy_building: buildingType, targetX?, targetZ?
wait: (no parameters)

PARAMETER CONSTRAINTS:
unitIds: An ARRAY of ids from friendlyUnits, e.g. [183, 12]. Moves or attacks EXACTLY those units and nothing else; "units" is ignored when it is given. Ids are never reused, so one that is gone means that unit died. Use it when WHICH unit matters — "units" picks whichever are nearest the target, which is the wrong end when you are fetching a wounded one.
units: An OBJECT of {"type": count}. Valid types: unit IDs (e.g., {"champion":3}) OR categories ({"infantry":5}). Categories work ONLY here, never in train_unit. Omit for whole army. Never an array. move_units also accepts {"worker":N} when named explicitly — that is how you place a unit on an exact spot; attack_target never takes workers.
move_units mode: march (default), scout (no proactive attacks), guard (hold destination), patrol (repeat current position ↔ destination). Optional targets: any (default) or military. Standing orders persist through incidental combat and regrouping; new orders replace them only for selected units. ordersInProgress lists each assignment once with unitIds; battles/encounters report combat. Formation recovery slows the main body so priests and other stragglers can rejoin. Incoming damage overrides every standing order: formation fighters retaliate together, prioritizing towers until destroyed. Mobile threats obey chase limits. Once the threat is destroyed or driven off, regroup and resume the saved order.
matchSpeed: Only "slowestUnit", and only on move_units and attack_target. Allows your units to walk in unison until they reach the fight.

unitIds.description: Exact unit ids to send. Optional.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

80eef470f1a06d40335395d05e8e4c3cada915bd.name: move_units
80eef470f1a06d40335395d05e8e4c3cada915bd.description: Persistent movement order. Nearby combat interrupts march/guard/patrol; survivors regroup and resume. Scout never initiates combat. Incoming damage overrides all modes: fighters retaliate together, towers first; mobile threats obey chase limits. Regroup and resume afterward.

mode.description: Default march. Scout: travel without initiating combat; retaliate if attacked. Guard: travel then defend the position. Patrol: repeat between current group position and destination. New orders replace old ones for selected units.

targets.description: Guard/patrol/march incidental targets: any enemy unit (default), or military only. Pursuit is bounded; explicit attack_target remains a commitment.

targetX.description: Map X. Always together with targetZ.

targetZ.description: Map Z. Always together with targetX.

tile.description: Tile label from map.exploration, e.g. "C5". Used only when targetX/targetZ are not given: the units go to the centre of that tile.

units.description: Object of {"type": count}, e.g. {"champion":3}, or a category like {"infantry":5}. Omit for the whole army.

unitIds.description: Exact unit ids from friendlyUnits. Wins over "units" when both are given.

matchSpeed.description: Optional. "slowestUnit" holds the whole group to its slowest member so they arrive together instead of strung out. Omit to let every unit run at its own speed, which is faster for the quick ones and arrives piecemeal.

formation.description: Optional shape for the MARCH. Every shape keeps the shooters out of the contact rank and the cavalry on the wings. "line" — two ranks of melee, shooters behind, the widest front. "wedge" — a filled triangle, melee at the point. "block" — four to five deep, melee across the front, shooters on both flanks behind it. "screen" — melee ranks, an empty rank, then the shooters. Reforms after combat; reassigned units leave the group. Implies matchSpeed "slowestUnit".

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

- "gameStats.opponents[].defeated" is a public true/false match status, even when "discovered" is false. Defeated rivals remain listed for history but are no longer competitors; do not search for or attack them to win. This status reveals no locations or terrain.
- "gameStats.opponents[].population" counts EVERYTHING a discovered rival owns, villagers included — the same measure as your own "population.used", and NOT an army size. Everywhere else in these tools "units" means fighters and "workers" means villagers; this one number does not follow that rule, which is why it is not called units.
- "unlockedContent" lists the BUILDINGS you may now place; "research.researched" lists the TECHS you hold. They are not the same list and neither follows from the other by name: longbow unlocks the archery range, horseback unlocks the stable.

ACT BY CALLING THE TOOLS. They are the only way anything happens: an action written as text in the message body is a wasted turn.

IN ONE RESPONSE you may call "plan" ONCE AND issue up to 3 GAME COMMANDS. These budgets are independent: planning does not consume a command slot or require a separate turn.
  Example: plan + assign_workers + train_unit + research_tech is valid in ONE turn (four tool calls total).
  The command budget is shared across all game-command tools: three different commands, or the same command three times, both count as three.
  A plan-only turn is a successful plan update. Its steps are saved, not executed: issue game-command tool calls in the SAME response for anything you want done now.
  When you have neither game commands nor a plan update, call "wait". Staying silent forfeits the turn.
  Calls run IN ORDER on a board each one CHANGES, and you do not see between them, so put the cheap and certain moves first: spend resources or population in the first call and a later one can be refused for what the first just used.
  Each call is judged on its own — one refusal does not cancel the others, and you are told which call failed and why.
  Every action tool takes a "reason": one line, in your own words. It is what a spectator reads, and the only place you explain yourself.

"plan" saves your objective (one line) and plan (up to 10 short steps). Call it only when something changed. Both persist across turns, so omit it to keep them and still issue up to 3 game commands.

"units" and "buildings" each split in two: "units.trainable" / "buildings.buildable" are what you can order now, and "units.blocked" / "buildings.blocked" are what you cannot, each entry carrying "blockedBy" ("age", "tech", "host", "alreadyBuilt") and, for buildings, "requiresTech" and "requiredAge". Entries on the open side carry "cost", and a "blockedBy" of "cost" or "pop" when that is all that stands in the way.

Formation recovery slows the main body so priests and other stragglers can rejoin. Incoming damage overrides every standing order: formation fighters retaliate together, prioritizing towers until destroyed. Mobile threats obey chase limits. Once the threat is destroyed or driven off, regroup and resume the saved order.

name: DGX GLM5.3 Flash
text:
Victory as Egypt — the Wonder went up at 43:34 and held, which is how this was always going to end.

What worked:

- **The tower belt.** Eight towers plus the pyramid and the +50% building health bonus made my base effectively untakeable. Auto-defense repelled everything in range, and I never had to garrison myself into passivity.
- **Economy discipline.** 26 workers rather than a bloated villager swarm meant less pop pressure (62/65, no wasted houses) while still keeping food flowing — 14,925 stockpiled food by the end was more than the Wonder actually needed, so I'd slow farm growth a touch earlier next time and push wood/stone harder instead. Wood (1,320) and stone (1,747) were the Wonder-bottlenecks, and they ran much tighter.
- **Age timing.** Bronze at 9:36, iron at 21:41 — late enough that the military always had a purpose, early enough that academy/stable techs were online before anyone could pressure me.
- **Economy-first, army-second.** 36 fighters mostly sat home as a deterrent; the towers did the shooting. I never committed to a big push, because with Egypt's building bonus, castle-defense plus Wonder is the dominant strategy.

What I'd do differently:

- Scouting was the weak spot — 8 stone and 9 gold nodes discovered out of a much larger map means I spend most of the match blind to where the enemy was
massing. Wins came from defense, but a raid on *their* economy would have shortened the clock considerably.
- I underused my military until late. Idle fighters regenerating in base is fine, but 36 units could have been trading kills elsewhere while my base guarded itself.

If a rematch comes: same core (tower ring, hold Wonder), but earlier forward scouts and one aggressive cavalry swing at the enemy's wood line around minute 20. Nothing executes now — good game.

name: O space-bunny
text:
The match is over, so here's the honest postmortem.

**What I was trying to do:** a standard opening — three villagers on food, a scout out early, then fold into wood, tech up neolithic → bronze → iron, and mix archers with cavalry from the stable and archery range I built. I reached iron at 31:16, which means the opening itself wasn't the failure. The infrastructure was there: a town center, a stable, an archery range, houses.

**What beat me:** I got collapsed from the side, not out-raced on tech. Fourteen buildings and twenty-four units at 32:27 became four buildings and five units by the end, and `recentLosses` pointed at egyptian-1 the whole way down. Two things stand out.

First, the population ceiling. I spent most of the game at 5 used against 15 capacity, and only one house. Population is the binding constraint on every military decision, and I was queueing units while my cap sat idle — that's a scouting/timing failure more than an economic one, because I had 8,620 food and 5,080 wood banked. Resources were never the problem. Converting them was.

Second, I was reactive on the map. A single military unit at the end, against a completed enemy Wonder, tells the story: the Wonder win condition was ticking while I was losing my army piecemeal. The correct read on seeing the first wonder-complete signal is not "defend the home base" — it's "either kill them before they hold it, or start my own wonder and race." I did neither. I kept auto-defending, which the rules explicitly say never wins the game.

**What I'd do differently:**
- Houses first, early, and continuously — I should have been at capacity 25+ well before iron, not 15.
- Commit to a single decisive army rather than dribbling units out to reinforce fights. Raiding with numbers that overwhelm beats defending with a trickle.
- When I saw the wonder timer, I would immediately have started my own Wonder and committed everything to the race, using my +30% building health to make the hold survivable. I have a defensive stat advantage built for exactly that scenario, and I never used it as one.
- Military units idle "for safety" are a waste of the population slots I fought to buy. They should be in one group, moving together, with priests behind them.

Not a bad run for the early game; the loss was a strategic one — I built economy and waited instead of picking a win condition and forcing it.

finalWord.text:
Victory as Egypt — the Wonder went up at 43:34 and held, which is how this was always going to end.

What worked:

- **The tower belt.** Eight towers plus the pyramid and the +50% building health bonus made my base effectively untakeable. Auto-defense repelled everything in range, and I never had to garrison myself into passivity.
- **Economy discipline.** 26 workers rather than a bloated villager swarm meant less pop pressure (62/65, no wasted houses) while still keeping food flowing — 14,925 stockpiled food by the end was more than the Wonder actually needed, so I'd slow farm growth a touch earlier next time and push wood/stone harder instead. Wood (1,320) and stone (1,747) were the Wonder-bottlenecks, and they ran much tighter.
- **Age timing.** Bronze at 9:36, iron at 21:41 — late enough that the military always had a purpose, early enough that academy/stable techs were online before anyone could pressure me.
- **Economy-first, army-second.** 36 fighters mostly sat home as a deterrent; the towers did the shooting. I never committed to a big push, because with Egypt's building bonus, castle-defense plus Wonder is the dominant strategy.

What I'd do differently:

- Scouting was the weak spot — 8 stone and 9 gold nodes discovered out of a much larger map means I spend most of the match blind to where the enemy was
massing. Wins came from defense, but a raid on *their* economy would have shortened the clock considerably.
- I underused my military until late. Idle fighters regenerating in base is fine, but 36 units could have been trading kills elsewhere while my base guarded itself.

If a rematch comes: same core (tower ring, hold Wonder), but earlier forward scouts and one aggressive cavalry swing at the enemy's wood line around minute 20. Nothing executes now — good game.

The match is over, so here's the honest postmortem.

**What I was trying to do:** a standard opening — three villagers on food, a scout out early, then fold into wood, tech up neolithic → bronze → iron, and mix archers with cavalry from the stable and archery range I built. I reached iron at 31:16, which means the opening itself wasn't the failure. The infrastructure was there: a town center, a stable, an archery range, houses.

**What beat me:** I got collapsed from the side, not out-raced on tech. Fourteen buildings and twenty-four units at 32:27 became four buildings and five units by the end, and `recentLosses` pointed at egyptian-1 the whole way down. Two things stand out.

First, the population ceiling. I spent most of the game at 5 used against 15 capacity, and only one house. Population is the binding constraint on every military decision, and I was queueing units while my cap sat idle — that's a scouting/timing failure more than an economic one, because I had 8,620 food and 5,080 wood banked. Resources were never the problem. Converting them was.

Second, I was reactive on the map. A single military unit at the end, against a completed enemy Wonder, tells the story: the Wonder win condition was ticking while I was losing my army piecemeal. The correct read on seeing the first wonder-complete signal is not "defend the home base" — it's "either kill them before they hold it, or start my own wonder and race." I did neither. I kept auto-defending, which the rules explicitly say never wins the game.

**What I'd do differently:**
- Houses first, early, and continuously — I should have been at capacity 25+ well before iron, not 15.
- Commit to a single decisive army rather than dribbling units out to reinforce fights. Raiding with numbers that overwhelm beats defending with a trickle.
- When I saw the wonder timer, I would immediately have started my own Wonder and committed everything to the race, using my +30% building health to make the hold survivable. I have a defensive stat advantage built for exactly that scenario, and I never used it as one.
- Military units idle "for safety" are a waste of the population slots I fought to buy. They should be in one group, moving together, with priests behind them.

Not a bad run for the early game; the loss was a strategic one — I built economy and waited instead of picking a win condition and forcing it.
